chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 14 of 21), named for no shrine: most confess the poet's bondage to courtesans and their embraces and ask for the feet, the gift of song or knowledge; others give the funeral and Death's crowd, a clause-by-clause inventory of old age, a mother's lament for her lovesick daughter, and in 1200 Murugan selling himself as Valli's slave. The praise turns on the churning of the ocean, the Mahabharata told almost whole, and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Courtesan and lovemaking songs (1190, 1191, 1193, 1195, 1197 to 1201); the funeral and death (1187, 1196); old age (1194); an akam lament in a mother's voice (1189); a plea for the One beyond the elements (1188); 1192 mixes the plea for mind's dissolution with Nakkirar's Tamil. Several songs (1191, 1194, 1201) end on Murugan as the one who taught Tamil or the silent Veda.

1187.reading: The poet pictures a life of walled mansions, gold in the house and many women around him, lived drunk and deluded, until on the last day the body is tied to the bier, friends wail and beat their chests and the limbed doll is given to the fire; he asks whether grace will not end this misery and set him holding Murugan's two sandals. The praise tells the churning of the sea with the golden mountain and the serpent rope, the poison that sent the gods into hiding, and Siva who held it, Murugan's father; it ends with his wooing of the hunter girl while the seven worlds laughed, and the heads of Sura cut off.
1187.nuance: இருபாதுகையைப் பற்றி நிற்க: the poet asks to hold Murugan's sandals (பாதுகை), not his feet, a humbler image of refuge. பாவை, 'doll', for the corpse makes the body a puppet once its life is gone. The line on the hunter girl and the laughing worlds is hard to divide, and its end is corrupt.

1188.reading: The poet asks for the One that Murugan spoke when Siva, who wears the bones of the dead, bowed to him, the thing that shines when the five elements, the inner instruments and the 'I' all subside; having reached desirelessness and fallen melting at the feet, he asks whether Murugan will not know that the cry 'Sentha, refuge, refuge' is never in vain. The praise tells of Vishnu who measured the worlds coming alone with the discus when the elephant in the pond cried 'Lord, my life is going', and ends with the peacock-like girl of the hills in the fragrant grove.
1188.nuance: நான்போய் ஒடுங்க அடங்கலும் மாய்ந்தால் விளங்கும் அது ஒன்றினை: the plea is for what appears only when the elements, the கரணங்கள் and the self are gone, a doctrinal request rather than a confession. வேண்டாமை, desirelessness, is named as already reached. The elephant's cry is Gajendra's.

1189.reading: In a mother's voice, the singer says her innocent girl is worn down by love: by the moon that rises like Death, the sleepless sea, the deceitful women who speak blame, the cowherd's flute, the cold north wind, Kama, and the bed that has turned strange; she asks Murugan, who once played the hunter to end the hunter girl's longing, to come on his two feet before her changed body wastes away. The praise names the six-faced lord of the vel, the peacock that holds Vasuki in its beak, and the release of the gods from Sura's prison.
1189.nuance: This is akam, the classical pangs of the lovesick girl spoken by her mother, as in 24: the moon, the sea, the wind and the herdsman's flute all wound her, and வசையே சொல் மாய மடவார், the gossiping women, are the town's blame (alar). The daughter's lover is the god himself.

1190.reading: The poet lists the charms of women who sell themselves, the trembling waist, pearl smile, curved brow, sugared speech, swan's walk, dark eyes and red mouth, and says that the karma which, while his mind lay degraded in them, made him think of the six-faced one is something he will never forget. The praise has Valli playing in the millet field, binding Murugan's twelve arms, and the golden mountain bent as a bow to burn the three cities of those who abandoned their vow.
1190.nuance: கண்ணழிவு வைத்த புத்தி ஷண்முக நினைக்க வைத்த கன்மவசம்: the poet appears to thank karma itself for turning his fallen mind toward Murugan, an unusual twist where the song ends in a vow (மறவேனே) rather than a request. The Tripura dwellers are called those who left the good vow (நல்வ்ரதத்தை விட்ட புன்மையர்).

1191.reading: The poet describes women who enforce Kama's command, melt young men, have spear eyes and 'thirty crore minds', and asks that, not ruined by them, he be granted to learn and recite Thiruppugazh and the knowledge of the tattvas in threefold Tamil. The praise names Siva who flayed the elephant, Vishnu as uncle, the vel that dried the sea against Sura, Valli embraced in the field, and Murugan who gives the true ascetics their life.
1191.nuance: திருப்புகழ் கற்கவும் ஓதவும்: the song asks for the book's own name, the praise of the Lord as a thing to learn and recite. முப்பது கோடி மனத்தியர், women of thirty crore minds, is the poet's figure for their fickleness.

1192.reading: The poet describes women whose hair, lips and spear eyes undo men, who drive them like the sea and make them seem mad, and whose embrace melts body and life like wax in fire, and asks that, with craving for the world removed, Murugan keep him and rule him at the golden feet where the mind is dissolved. The praise recalls the vel that stretched out for the Tamil of Nakkirar at the Madurai Koodal hill, Murugan's search for the hunter girl, and the moment when, to please moon-crowned Siva, he sent his peacock round the world.
1192.nuance: மனோலயம், dissolution of the mind, occurs twice: first in the women's embrace, then at the feet the poet asks for, as if the same melting were sought in its true place. நக்கீரர் ஓதிய தமிழுக்காக நீடிய கரவோனே: the hand stretched out for Nakkirar's Tamil, the poet of Murugan's own praise. The peacock sent round the world in an instant points to the contest for the fruit, though the fruit is not named. Several runs in the first half are hard to divide.

1193.reading: The poet describes women with cloth over their breasts, crescent brows and eyes blacked with collyrium, whom he sought out until his heart, infatuated and scattered, could not join Murugan's work, and asks whether this deceit will never leave him. The praise names Murugan as companion of the devotees who praise him steadily through tapas, bridegroom of Devayanai born for the gods' welfare, and the vel that broke the mountain and defeated Sura who came hidden in a deceiving form.
1193.nuance: நின்செயல் மருவாமல் கலங்கும் வஞ்சகம்: the deceit is the poet's own, a heart that will not join the Lord's work. Lines 5 and 6 (விநன்முசிப், வன்சர மென்முவா) appear garbled.

1194.reading: The poet sets out old age clause by clause: strength gone, pride broken, years spent, teeth fallen, back bent like a bow, face dimmed, sight darkened, cough come, sleep gone, speech failing, tongue fallen, mind fading, limbs that will not stretch, diseases lodged, the mat reached and the stench of filth risen, and says 'now it is a matter of a moment, come before me in grace'. The praise has the vel thrown against the demons who imprisoned Indra, Valli wooed in the millet field and married in the sight of the world, and Murugan who expounded clear Sentamil to his devotees.
1194.nuance: Each clause ends in அது (ஒழிந்தது, உதிர்ந்தது, வளைந்தது), so the decay is told as a running inventory, one verb at a time. நிமிஷம் இங்கு இனி ஆச்சுது: the plea is for grace at the very last minute, with no confession of women.

1195.reading: The poet confesses wandering round the lies of petty women who teach Kama's arts with their carp eyes and draw men to perfumed golden beds, calls himself base, and asks for the one day when Murugan will make him fit, teach him to worship his feet and grant his mind grace. The praise, in drum syllables, shows Siva's dance and calls Murugan the guru who gave grace to siddhas, the pure freed ones and devotees, the destroyer of Tripura's demons who freed the gods, with the cock banner.
1195.nuance: உனதடி அர்ச்சிக்க: what the poet asks to be taught is ritual worship of the feet. The battle lines (திக்குக்குத் திகுதிகு, டுட்டுட்டு) are rhythm, not words.

1196.reading: The poet pictures Death with a crore of spears pressing to waste his life while the women he loved still cling, and the elders and young saying 'what's left to do, is he dead?', carrying him to the burning ground and saying he will fall into the seven hells, a wretch without fortune; he asks Murugan to come with the Vedas sounding while the worlds, the gods and the sages praise him. The praise retells the Mahabharata: Dharma losing the land at dice, twelve years in the forest, the stay at Virata's court and the cattle raid, the embassy, Duryodhana's death in the war, and Vishnu who drove Arjuna's chariot, Murugan's uncle.
1196.nuance: ஏது கருமம் இவர் சாவெனா: the kin's words over the dying man are quoted, coldly practical. இருவாறு வருஷம், two sixes of years, is the Pandavas' twelve-year exile; the praise gives the epic in sequence rather than as single epithets.

1197.reading: The poet, beaten about by women whose mouths drip honey and whose sulks are their gift, calls himself a sinful utter fool and asks on what day, before he becomes the work of misfortune, Murugan will grant him the work of his service. The praise names Vishnu whose arrows scattered Ravana's crowns, Murugan's uncle, and the lord who lived with the hunter girl in the small hut of the forest people.
1197.nuance: முகடித் தொழில் against அடிமைத் தொழில்: the work of Mudevi, goddess of ill fortune, set against the work of service to the Lord, if முகடி is read so. ஆகாஎ நாளினில் is probably a garble of ஆக எந்நாளினில்.

1198.reading: The poet describes plainly his nights with common women, the necklace, the betel-reddened lips, the loosened silk, and says that even while his mind practises the arts of love he will not forget the sword in Murugan's hand, the protection of his golden feet adorned with vetchi flowers, and his jewelled anklets. The praise is a battlefield: demon cities burned, asuras pierced, and countless ghouls dragging corpses, drumming and laughing while birds fly.
1198.nuance: மறவேனே: as in 1007 the song ends with a vow of remembrance inside the passion, not a plea for escape from it.

1199.reading: The poet describes the common women who show their hair, breasts and peacock walk and kindle infatuation with thrilling words, and asks Murugan to drive out and change the base nature that craves a life fit for them. The praise names the devotees who praise his radiant feet with instruments, the women who fed and played with the child Murugan, the god who scattered the fools' clan with a smile and restored the gods' song, and the guru who saw the poet's trouble and rescued him by showing him his two deeds.
1199.nuance: இருவினை காட்டி மீட்ட: rescue comes by being shown one's own two kinds of deed. ஆய்ச்சிமார், cowherd women, who feed and bathe the child are hard to identify; they may be the foster-mothers of Murugan's birth or a borrowing from Krishna's story.

1200.reading: The poet asks whether he should be caught in the deceiving net of play-acting dancing women, called a madman by the whole world, losing shame, custom, conduct, justice and sense, and become the slave of the slaves of dogs. The praise answers with Murugan's own servitude: to the hunter girl dressed in peacock feathers and leaves on the platform with her sling, he said 'I am your hereditary slave', clasped her feet again and again, and with the Vedas, the gods and the world's rim as witness sold himself and had it written on Meru.
1200.nuance: The two halves mirror each other: the poet fears becoming a slave (நாயடிமையும் அடிமைப்பட்டு) to women of deceit, while the god freely declares himself Valli's வழியடிமை, sold (விலைப்பட்டு) by a deed inscribed on Meru. Bondage to desire and bondage in love are set side by side.

1201.reading: After a long and frank picture of lovemaking until the two seem one, the poet asks that even in the days when his mind is lost in that passion he be given ways to praise Murugan's two feet, the vel hand that casts out karma, his holy face beyond depicting, and his grace. The praise has Vishnu and Brahma pressing his feet, a battlefield of ghouls, vultures and Bhairavas, and calls Murugan the supreme guru who showed the Lord of the matted hair the silent way that the ancient Veda gives.
1201.nuance: எனது மனது அழியும் நாட்களினும் ... ஏத்தும் வகை தரவேணும்: praise is asked for within the passion, not after it. பழய மறை தரு மவுன வழி: what Murugan teaches Siva is named here as the silent way of the Veda, without Om.

links.note: Both are a mother's lament for a daughter lovesick for Murugan, worn by the moon, the wind and the evening; 24 adds the anril bird, 1189 the gossiping women and the herdsman's flute.
The herdsman's flute as a weapon of evening: the Kural's woman calls it a messenger of the burning dusk that kills, and in 1189 the cowherd's flute is among the things wearing the girl down.

The Naladiyar sketches the old man whose speech fails and teeth fall but who still keeps his eyes on desire; 1194 lists every stage of that decay down to the stench of the sickbed and turns it into a plea for grace at the last moment.

source_issues: 1187: the line before the last ends with a stray '....... ;' before ளையோனே (probably இளையோனே).
1188: the glyph ஡ stands for ஊ in ஞான்று஡து (ஞான்றூது, line 17); வீழந்தாவல் for வீழ்ந்தாவல் (line 9).
1189: the glyph ஡ stands for ஊ in குழலு஡தி (குழலூதி, line 3); சூரர்அகாடு (line 15) appears garbled.
1193: lines 5 and 6 (விநன்முசிப், வன்சர மென்முவா) appear garbled.
1197: ஆகாஎ நாளினில் probably for ஆக எந்நாளினில்.
1195: initial உ split from its word (உ ற்பித்து).
